evidence.text: To stop someone 止 with an arrow 弋
楚莊王曰：“夫武，定功戢兵。故止戈爲武。”

Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 戈 (“blade”) + 止 (“foot; to walk; to stop”) – army going on an expedition. In the character 武, the 戈 component is written above the 止 component.
The graphical origin of 武 as “to stop violence” — the ultimate state of just warfare — is traditionally attributed to King Zhuang of Chu [597 BCE]:
Linguistically, this was likely a misinterpretation, as 止 always means “to walk” (趾) when used as a radical, compare 步 (bù), 歷 /历 (lì) and 歧 (qí).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *d-maq (“war, army, soldier”). Cognate with Tibetan དམག (dmag, “army”), Burmese မက် (mak) (as in ရဲမက် (rai:mak, “soldier”) (STEDT; Schuessler, 2007; Sagart, 2017d).
楚莊王曰：“夫武，定功戢兵。故止戈爲武。”

Oracle 武 combines the weapon 戈 and foot-shaped 止, interpreted as an armed force advancing. Bronze uses include military affairs and martial strength. The traditional “stop weapons” interpretation expresses an ethical ideal, but need not be the original construction because early 止 often indicates walking.
evidence.title: 武 — historical form and meaning

evidence.source: Japan Kanji Aptitude Testing Foundation / Atsuji Tetsuji
evidence.text: Early 武 combines pictures of a 戈 weapon and a foot or footprint represented by 止, interpreted as armed advance. The clerical and modern regular-script shapes no longer divide cleanly into the separately written 戈 and 止. 戈 depicts a long-handled weapon with an angled blade.
